full_judgment:
2. The prosecution case in brief is that on the 11th Ashar, 1375 B.S. (corresponding to 25-6-1968) the accused respondents along with others cut and took away half ripe aush paddy worth about Taka 500/- grown by the complainant Shahjahan Mia on his own land being Plot Nos.199 and 279 of Mouza Bowla and thereby committed an offence under section 379 of the Penal Code. The said lands formerly belonged to one Hitu Mudi who was recorded to have been in exclusive possession of the same in the record of right prepared under the cadastral survey (Ext.4) and were subsequently acquired by one Balaram Das, on the basis of a deed of purchase dated 14-11-1919 (Ext. 2) and an auction purchase in a court sale as evidenced by the sale certificate dated 29-11-1919 (Ext. 3). Balaram Das got his name recorded in respect of the said lands in the record of right prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Ext. 5) and paid rent on the basis of the rent receipt Ext. 6 series. Haji Jahiruddin, the late father of the complainant, who was a refugee from Assam, got possession of the said lands on the basis of an unregistered deed of exchange dated 20-3-64 (Ext.1), and got his name mutated in the office of the Government Acquired Estate and paid rent in respect of the said lands for several years as shown by rent receipts Ext. 7 series. The paddy in question was grown by the complainant on his own land which was in his exclusive possession. 

 15. The complete want of bonafide in respect of the claim urged on behalf of the accused persons will be apparent on a close examination of their claim of the right to possess the land itself, about which the High Court appears to have taken a favorable view. The basis of the claim seems to be the record of right of Cadastral Survey (Ext. 4), in which the disputed land was described as 'Jote Bishu Mudi' but was recorded in exclusive possession of Hitu Mudi, the son. Shortly after the publication of this record Balaram went into exclusive possession of the said land partly on the basis of a kabala from Hitu Mudi (Ext.2), and partly on the basis of an auction purchase of the interest of Hitu Mudi and another person in court a sale (Ext. 3) in November. 1919. The tenancy and possession in respect of the said land, were thereafter recorded exclusively in the name of Balaram in the record of rights prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Ext. 5) and rent receipts granted by the office of the Government Acquired Estate (Ext. 6 series) show that it was Balaram who alone paid the rent of the tenancy for the years 1363 B.S.,-1366 B.S. Balaram appears to have exchanged all his properties including the disputed land with the properties of the father of the complainant, lying in the Indian State of Assam and in token thereof an unregistered deed of exchange (Ext.1) between the parties was executed on 20-3-1964. It is true that this deed was unregistered, and it may be well argued that the title of the complainants father was not complete by virtue of this deed, but it is well established it is the concurrent finding of the lower Courts-that the complainants father had gone into exclusive possession of the disputed land on the basis of the said deed of exchange, got his name mutated in the office of the Govt. Acquired Estate and paid rent, in his own name, for the years, 1371 B.S. to 1374 B.S., i.e., up to the year 1967-68 on the basis of the rent receipt Exts. 7 series. From the finding arrived at in the case, it is clear that Balaram, who was a stranger to the family of Bishu Mudi had been exclusively in possession of the disputed land for a continuous period of about 45 years, and thereafter the complainant and his father had been in possession for a further period of about 5 years before the date of the disputed occurrence.
